title: Some Problems with To Dos, Big Questions, I Dos and Exit Tickets in English Classrooms
author: Didau, David
summary: Didau traces how English state schools converged, almost overnight between 2020 and 2023, on a five-part lesson template — To Do, Big Question, I Do, independent practice, Exit Ticket — and argues the convergence happened through informal channels (instructional coaching, multi-academy-trust frameworks, Rosenshine-influenced CPD) rather than any government mandate. He locates each ingredient's genealogy: the 'I Do' from Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction and Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion, the Exit Ticket from Assessment for Learning, and the Big Question from inquiry-based learning's desire to give lessons a hook. His real argument is critical: the Big Question often becomes a compliance ritual rather than a genuine driver of learning, gets written for the whiteboard rather than to fit the curriculum, and doesn't transfer cleanly into subjects like PE, art, or languages. He closes with a historian's shrug — this is simply the latest repackaging of the three-part lesson, and it too will eventually be renamed and rediscovered.
points: The now-standard English lesson template spread nationally through academy-trust frameworks and CPD networks, not through any Ofsted or DfE requirement.
The Big Question is often written to satisfy a display or a learning walk rather than to genuinely organize a lesson's content.
A 'big question' can actively distract from precise procedural or vocabulary learning, especially in subjects like maths.
The template doesn't map cleanly onto PE, art, or modern languages, where skill or self-expression — not a conceptual question — is the point.
Didau predicts the cycle will repeat: every pedagogical era repackages the same core moves under new names.
quotes: This sequence has become so embedded in English schools that many teachers barely notice they're using it.
The shift to the newer sequence happened fast, and it wasn't introduced by the Department for Education, Ofsted, or any national body.
Many schools adopt Big Questions because they look good in planning documents or on classroom displays. I think that a question on a board doesn't necessarily drive the learning.

For example, in maths, a conceptual question like "Is zero a number or an idea?" can overshadow the actual procedural learning needed in that lesson, and in knowledge-heavy subjects (history, science), Big Questions can feel like an unnecessary layer on top of already complex content.
But Ofsted does not require Big Questions, and this misunderstanding can lead to teachers overpreparing for an inspection at a cost to their physical and mental health.
If you've been in teaching long enough, you'll know that nothing is ever really new. So for instance, the three-part lesson was once revolutionary and before that, it was chalk and talk.
